extracted.intended_audience: mathematics students, instructors, and authors preparing mathematical writing and presentations
extracted.subtask_description: A curated collection of handouts and links giving guidance and standards for writing mathematics papers, proofs, abstracts, and for preparing and delivering mathematical presentations; aimed at helping students and instructors improve communication and assessment in mathematics. Covers organization, style, proofs, notation, presentations, and pedagogy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be considerate of your audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Tailor exposition to the intended audience; choose level of detail, vocabulary, and motivation appropriate to readers or listeners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appears as explicit advice ("Be considerate of your audience"). Linked resources (e.g., John M. Lee's remarks, Maurer, undergraduate guides) discuss audience, clarity, motivation, precision, and level of detail; orienting material and 'Guiding the audience through the content' pages provide concrete strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordering information so content flows logically
rubrics_metrics.description: Arrange material so the reader can follow the development; order definitions, lemmas, examples, and motivation to build understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed under 'Information Order and Connectivity' and 'Guiding the audience through the content'; includes annotated introductions and recommendations to integrate section references into introductions rather than deferring them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure of a mathematical paper (parts and introductions)
rubrics_metrics.description: A mathematical paper should have clear parts (introduction, main results, proofs, discussion) with introductions that state problem, significance, relation to literature, and roadmap.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple resources (Steenrod/Halmos/Schiffer/Dieudonne, Reiter, Krantz, 'The Art of Writing Introductions' article) emphasize introductions that define the problem and synthesize significance; 'Writing a Research Paper in Mathematics' lists 14 recommendations including a clear definition of the problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Get to the point / concision
rubrics_metrics.description: Make exposition direct and avoid unnecessary verbiage; present main ideas early and avoid burying the point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted advice from Jonathan Shewchuk: 'Get to the point!' and recommendation that section references be folded into the introduction so the logical place of each statement is clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclusions should synthesize results
rubrics_metrics.description: Conclusions must synthesize what was achieved and separate what is significant from what is not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shewchuk's advice specifically: 'Conclusions should synthesize the results of your paper and separate what is significant from what is not.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision and rigor
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure definitions, statements, and proofs meet standards of mathematical precision and logical rigor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed under 'Precision and rigor' and reinforced by resources about rigor, proofs, and 'How to Write Mathematics'; Haynes Miller's notes mention distinguishing belief from proof and a list of common errors affecting precision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof structure and proof-writing strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose appropriate proof types and structure proofs so they are readable: state strategy, give motivation, break into clear steps, and indicate where standard results are used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covered in 'Types of proof & proof-writing strategies', 'Proof Structure', 'Proof Elegance', and handouts like 'Some Remarks on Writing Mathematical Proofs' and annotated examples ('Maximum Overhang').

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof elegance
rubrics_metrics.description: Seek clarity and simplicity in proofs; prefer proofs that illuminate ideas rather than just verify facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as a topic; resources discuss what makes proofs elegant and how to present elegant arguments to aid reader understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balancing conceptual and formal exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Balance informal conceptual explanations with formal definitions and proofs so readers gain intuition as well as correctness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as 'Balancing conceptual with formal' and appears across resources that advise blending motivation and formalism rather than one or the other exclusively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrating equations, text, and figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Integrate displayed mathematics, running text, and figures so that notation and formulas are introduced, explained, and referenced naturally in the flow of exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Referenced via annotated articles and handouts (e.g., 'Maximum Overhang' annotated, 'How to integrate equations, text, and figures') and practical guides for student papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notation use and consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose clear notation, define it before use, and maintain consistency throughout the document.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resources include 'The Use of Symbols: A Case Study', pages on 'notation', and 'Wording and punctuation' discussing when to punctuate displays and how to refer to symbols.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wording, punctuation, and grammatical mechanics
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow standards of English usage (articles, comma usage, sentence structure) and mathematical punctuation; avoid common grammatical errors that impede clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Haynes Miller's notes list 15 common errors (articles, comma splices); general references include Strunk & White and Chicago Manual of Style; 'Wording and punctuation' page gives guidance on punctuation of displays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific small-scale style rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt recommended small-scale conventions (e.g., avoid using 'any'; prefer 'each' or 'every' where appropriate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From 'Writing a Research Paper in Mathematics' recommendations: concrete rules such as 'never use "any" in mathematical writing. Replace it by "each" or "every".'

rubrics_metrics.name: Using sources, citation, and attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Cite prior work appropriately, indicate what is new, and follow disciplinary conventions for attribution and references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pages on 'Using sources', 'Writing for Mathematical Reviews', and notes on attribution (Haynes Miller) discuss citation norms and distinguishing belief from proof; also references to authorship dispute guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship and ethical considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow community norms for authorship, acknowledgements, and dispute resolution; understand discipline-specific conventions (e.g., alphabetical authorship).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resource 'How to handle authorship disputes' is recommended as a starting point; the page notes mathematics convention of alphabetical authorship and suggests careful consideration of authorship decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Readability and intelligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Write to make mathematics intelligible: choose good terminology, exposition style, and examples so readers can follow arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References such as R. P. Boas 'Can We Make Mathematics Intelligible?' and other essays discuss pitfalls in terminology, symbolism, and presentation that harm intelligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Titles and first impressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose article titles that accurately reflect content and attract appropriate readership; 'Article Titles Make a Difference.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed resource emphasizes title selection as an important part of communicating and positioning work for readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparing results for publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Present results in publishable form: polish exposition, follow journal conventions, and prepare clear abstracts and introductions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notices AMS pieces like 'Preparing Your Results for Publication' and guides on writing referee reports and 'How to write your first paper' provide concrete steps for preparing manuscripts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing abstracts
rubrics_metrics.description: Compose concise abstracts that state the problem, main results, and significance in a way accessible to intended audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Student guide to writing an abstract (Ivars Peterson) is linked; general advice across the collection on abstracts and introductions applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revising, incremental drafts, and peer critique
rubrics_metrics.description: Use incremental drafting and peer critique to improve clarity and correctness; allow revision cycles informed by feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Site sections: 'Incremental drafts', 'Revising Writing', 'Peer critique on writing', and 'Sample critiques' provide methods, sample instructor comments, and exercises to structure feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment and objective grading of communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop rubrics and criteria to assess writing and presentations objectively despite subjective elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page asks 'How can I objectively grade something as subjective as communication?' and links to assessment resources, checklists, and grade rubrics for writing in math classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignments and scaffolding for student writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Design writing assignments (e.g., abstracts, term papers, research reports) with clear formatting and content expectations, sequencing, and instructor feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resources include assignment examples (personal essay, biographical sketch, notebooks, 3–5 page research papers), formatting requirements, sample drafts with instructor responses, and sequencing advice (e.g., 'Writing in Introduction to Euclidean Geometry').

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentations: characteristics of effective talks
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective student talks have clear structure, appropriate pacing, audience engagement, and use of visuals aligned with spoken exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covered in 'Characteristics of effective student talks and papers', 'Engaging the audience', 'Practice presentations', and 'Sample presentations: examples & cautions'; includes peer critique for presentations and practice exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presenting to learn: using speaking as a learning tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Oral presentation and discussion can reinforce understanding; structure talks to promote student learning rather than mere reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed under 'Presenting to learn: learning math by talking about it' and 'Using communication to help reduce math anxiety'; resources discuss activities and seminar designs that use presentations pedagogically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using visuals and figures effectively
rubrics_metrics.description: Design figures and visual aids to clarify concepts, avoid clutter, label clearly, and integrate them with text and spoken explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resources on 'Using visuals', 'LaTeX labels on figures', and sample presentation handouts discuss cautions and examples for figure use.

rubrics_metrics.name: LaTeX and technical presentation tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Use LaTeX (and front-ends like LyX) appropriately: templates, skeleton files, figure labels, and advanced typesetting for clear presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides LaTeX skeletons for articles and problem sets, 'Advanced LaTeX Topics', 'LaTeX resource list', and 'LaTeX handout for novices' to standardize formatting and ease production of readable documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative writing and using data/examples as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: When mathematics involves data or quantitative argumentation, present numerical evidence, examples, and computations clearly and relate them to formal claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed under 'Quantitative writing and presentations' and 'Evidence can also be supplied by examples and data' in the Writing Lexicon mapping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidance for English learners and global English
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide advice and resources tailored to non-native English speakers to help them communicate mathematics effectively in global contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The site has a dedicated page for 'English learners & global English' and points to resources (OWL, ESL guides) suitable for multilingual writers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of good mathematical writing and annotated exemplars
rubrics_metrics.description: Study annotated examples (e.g., annotated 'Maximum Overhang') to learn how introductions, integration of equations, citations, and guidance of reader are handled in exemplary papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page links to award-winning articles with annotations pointing out structure, integration of equations and figures, citation practice, and how to guide readers.
